title: The Nolan's Circle: Nola to Campo de' Fiori, the Infinite Universe and the Fire
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Nola and the Cloister of Naples

stops.name: Nola, the house below Cicala, birth and baptism
stops.campa: In the small Campanian city of Nola, under the shadow of Vesuvius and the lesser slope of Monte Cicala, a boy is born to Giovanni Bruno, a soldier of modest means, and Fraulisa Savolino, and is baptized Filippo. The volcano stands always in view, and the wide, fertile plain around the city, planted with vine and olive, will stay with him as the remembered ground of thought itself: he will speak of Nola again and again in the books written on the far side of the Alps, of the Thames and the Elbe, homesick for this one particular light.
suggested_refs: The house of Giovanni Bruno at Nola, beneath Monte Cicala, birthplace of the Nolan
Vesuvius seen from Nola, the horizon of his childhood and of his cosmology
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Bruno, Giordano'

stops.name: Naples, letters, logic, and dialectic
stops.campa: At about fourteen the boy is sent to Naples to study the humanities, logic, and dialectic, lodging and learning under the private tutors called il Sarnese and, above all, the Augustinian friar Teofilo da Vairano, who opens to him the arts of memory and the combinatory logic of Ramon Llull, the Catalan master dead two and a half centuries but newly urgent again. In Teofilo's rooms the boy first handles Llull's wheels of concepts turning within concepts, the seed of a method he will carry, transformed, through every court of Europe.
suggested_refs: Ramon Llull's Ars combinatoria, the revolving wheels of concepts first shown him by Teofilo da Vairano
sources: Marco Matteoli, 'Ars combinatoria and Ars memoriae in Giordano Bruno'

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore, the habit of the Order
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of July, seventeen years old, Filippo enters the great Dominican convent of San Domenico Maggiore as a novice cleric and takes, in religion, the name Giordano, after the Roman martyr of the Dominican calendar. Within these cloisters, once the school of Aquinas himself, he is given the full apparatus of scholastic philosophy and the freedom of a library stocked with condemned and half-condemned books. He conceals, against the order of the general chapter, a copy of the Fathers with the Erasmian annotations struck through by other hands but still legible beneath the strokes.
suggested_refs: The cloister of San Domenico Maggiore, Naples, where Filippo became Fra Giordano
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

stops.name: Campagna, ordination and the first Mass at San Bartolomeo
stops.campa: Subdeacon, then deacon, Fra Giordano is consecrated priest once he has turned twenty-four, and is sent inland from Naples to say his first Mass in the Dominican house of San Bartolomeo at Campagna, above the Sele valley near Salerno. He is already remarked on: a memory that returns long passages after a single hearing, a tongue too quick for comfort in disputation. Earlier he has been sent to Rome to demonstrate his mnemonic art before Pope Pius V and Cardinal Rebiba, a brief public triumph that will not save him, for the same gift for saying exactly what he thinks is already collecting enemies inside the convent walls.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent church of San Bartolomeo at Campagna, near Salerno, where Fra Giordano said his first Mass
The mnemonic demonstration Fra Giordano gave before Pope Pius V, cited in his own trial testimony
sources: Documenti del processo, Archivio della Congregazione per la Dottrina della Fede

stops.name: Naples, the scholia of Erasmus and the heresy of Arius
stops.campa: Word reaches the Provincial that Fra Giordano has argued the Arian heresy against the Trinity in dispute with Fra Agostino da Montalcino, and has kept, against express prohibition, a copy of Chrysostom and Jerome with Erasmus's scholia scraped but not erased. A trial for heresy opens in Naples at the start of the year. Warned that arrest is coming, Giordano throws off the outward peace of the cloister he has worn for eleven years, sheds the white-and-black habit within weeks of the summons, and rides north before the Holy Office can close its hand on him.
suggested_refs: The forbidden Erasmus scholia, scraped but legible, that opened the first heresy file against him
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

segments.name: The Wandering Apostate: Rome to the Alps

stops.name: Rome, Santa Maria sopra Minerva, the habit set aside
stops.campa: He reaches Rome and asks shelter of his own order at the great Dominican house of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, still, technically, a friar in good standing outside Naples. But the Neapolitan file follows him north within weeks, thickened now with the report of a brother found drowned and old suspicion of foul play laid, unfairly or not, at his door. Giordano does not wait to be summoned a second time. He lays aside the white scapular of Saint Dominic for good, puts on the plain clothes of a wandering scholar, and turns north, a fugitive from his own vocation at twenty-eight.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, where the Nolan's cowl was laid aside for the last time

stops.name: Noli, teaching grammar and the sphere for bread
stops.campa: Without habit, benefice, or protector, the ex-friar earns his keep as any masterless scholar must: at Noli on the Ligurian coast he teaches grammar to the town's boys for four months, and, for the local gentry curious about the heavens, gives lessons on Sacrobosco's sphere and the ordering of the planets. He will later tell his Venetian judges of these humble months plainly, without shame: a doctor of theology reduced to the schoolroom of children, and glad of the wage. From Noli he crosses to Savona, then inland to Turin, mapping in his own body the roads of an Italy too small now to hold him.
stops.quote: I went to Noli, on the Genoese riviera, and stayed there four months, teaching grammar to boys and reading the Sphere to certain gentlemen.
stops.quote_source: Venetian trial deposition, 1592 (Documenti del processo, ed. Firpo), in translation
suggested_refs: Sacrobosco's De sphaera, the schoolbook of the stars Bruno taught for his bread at Noli
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

stops.name: Venice, a small book on the signs of the times
stops.campa: The wandering scholar reaches Venice, city of presses free enough to print what Rome would burn, and has struck off a small treatise, De' segni de' tempi, on the signs and portents of the age: it does not survive, but its title alone marks a mind already reading the heavens as a text of prophecy and change rather than a fixed Aristotelian ceiling. He does not linger; the lagoon is a way-station, not a refuge, and within weeks he is on the road again westward, toward Padua and the university towns of the Veneto and Lombardy.
suggested_refs: De' segni de' tempi, Bruno's first known printed work, now lost

stops.name: Padua and Bergamo, the Dominicans who begged him back
stops.campa: At Padua, Dominican brothers of his own order recognize the fugitive and urge him to resume the habit and the observance, at least outwardly, the better to travel safely; he puts it on again for a season, a pragmatist's compromise, and lodges a while at Bergamo. But the compromise cannot hold a mind already loosed from every enclosure. Within the year he sheds the habit again, this time for good, and turns toward the mountains: Milan, then the Alpine passes, aiming for the Calvinist cantons where, whatever else awaits him, the Roman Inquisition's arm does not reach.
suggested_refs: The Dominican house at Bergamo, last place the habit was worn

stops.name: Chambéry and the crossing into Geneva
stops.campa: He crosses by Chambéry in Savoy, resting briefly among monks who receive him as a curiosity more than a guest, and is advised by a French nobleman he meets on the road that a former friar traveling in his own habit through reformed country invites suspicion from both sides at once: better to go as a plain man. He takes the advice, and in the last months of the year passes the frontier into the Calvinist republic of Geneva, city of Calvin's memory and of presses that will, for a season, need a proofreader more than they need a confession of faith.
suggested_refs: The Alpine road from Chambéry to Geneva, the frontier of Bruno's confessional wandering

stops.name: Geneva, proofreader in Calvin's city
stops.campa: In Geneva, capital of a Reformation that is not his own, Giordano sets aside every outward mark of Rome, is received among the Italian exile congregation, and takes work correcting proof for the city's printers, the trade of many a displaced scholar. On the twentieth of May he matriculates at the Genevan Academy, entered in the rector's book as Filippo Bruno of Nola. For a few months it seems the fugitive might make a life here, among fellow Italians who fled the Inquisition before him: a proofreader's quiet, after three years on the road.
suggested_refs: The rector's book of the Genevan Academy, 20 May 1579, entering 'Filippo Bruno nolano'

stops.name: Geneva, the pamphlet against La Faye, and the excommunication
stops.campa: His tongue betrays him again. Giordano has a broadsheet printed listing twenty errors he claims to find in a single lecture of Antoine de la Faye, professor of philosophy and pillar of the Calvinist Academy: it is read as defamation of a magistrate of the faith. On the thirteenth of August the consistory tries him and finds him guilty, all but excommunicate; after a weak defense he bends, confesses fault, and begs readmission to the sacrament. On the twenty-seventh he is absolved. But the episode leaves a scar of anti-Calvinist anger that will surface again and again in the books written after, and Geneva no longer wants him.
suggested_refs: The consistory record of Geneva, 13 August 1579, Bruno's trial for defaming Antoine de la Faye

stops.name: Toulouse, the doctorate and the chair on the soul
stops.campa: He crosses into Catholic France, to Toulouse, and there, license and past unmentioned, takes a doctorate in theology and wins by competition the ordinary lectureship in philosophy. For very nearly two years he lectures publicly on Aristotle's De Anima, the treatise on the soul, teaching within the letter of the school while privately already doubting its walls: an earth that does not move, a heaven of crystal spheres, a cosmos closed like a shell around a single sun. Students crowd to hear a lecturer whose memory needs no text before him.
suggested_refs: The lecture hall of the University of Toulouse, where Bruno taught De Anima for two years

stops.name: Toulouse, the wars of religion close the schools
stops.campa: In the summer, the truce between Catholic Toulouse and its Huguenot countryside breaks again into open war, as it has broken and mended a dozen times in this generation; the university empties, lecture halls stand idle, and the philosopher without a party in either camp judges it time to move again. He turns north to Paris, city of a king who has already heard, by report, of an Italian doctor whose memory performs like a conjuring trick and whose lectures on the sphere leave the schoolmen uneasy.
suggested_refs: The Wars of Religion in Languedoc, 1581, that emptied the University of Toulouse

stops.name: Paris, the reputation that reaches Henri III
stops.campa: Paris receives the wandering Nolan into a court fascinated by exactly his kind of gift: Henri III himself, a king who collects magi, cabalists, and memory-artists the way other princes collect relics, sends for him and has him demonstrate before the whole assembled court an art of memory that lets him repeat, forward or backward, whole strings of names and words heard only once. The king asks whether the trick is natural skill or forbidden magic; Bruno answers that it is neither sorcery but a science, built on Ramon Llull's wheels and on his own reworking of them, and offers to teach it in print.
stops.quote: This memory of mine is not by magic, but by science.
stops.quote_source: Bruno's own account, given later to the Venetian inquisitors, of his reply to Henri III
suggested_refs: The court of Henri III at the Louvre, where the art of memory was demonstrated before the king
sources: Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition

stops.name: Paris, De umbris idearum laid before the king
stops.campa: From the press of Gilles Gourbin comes De umbris idearum, On the Shadows of Ideas, bound with the Ars memoriae and dedicated to His Most Christian Majesty: a book that fuses Ficino's Neoplatonic psychology, Llull's combinatorial wheels, and a hermetic doctrine of shadow-images through which the mind climbs from sense toward the intelligible sun. Bruno tells his judges afterward, plainly, what came of it: printed and dedicated to the king, the book earns him appointment as an extraordinary and paid lecturer, a post outside the ordinary faculty, since he will not attend the Mass required of a full chair.
stops.quote: After this I had a book on memory printed, under the title De Umbris Idearum, which I dedicated to his majesty; and on this occasion he made me an extraordinary and paid lecturer.
suggested_refs: De umbris idearum, Paris 1582, the shadow-wheel diagrams of the art of memory

stops.name: Paris, Il Candelaio and the comedy of the age
stops.campa: The same year, Bruno lets loose Il Candelaio, The Torchbearer, a five-act comedy conceived years before in Naples and now printed at Paris: a riotous, obscene, learned satire of an alchemist, a pedant, and a lovesick miser, its Italian larded with Neapolitan slang and mock-Latin, its prologue already announcing the philosopher's contempt for a corrupt and credulous age. It is his only play, and his most Neapolitan book, written in the city of kings by a man who has not stopped being the boy from under Vesuvius.
suggested_refs: Il Candelaio, Paris 1582, Bruno's sole comedy, printed by Guglielmo Giuliano
sources: pensierofilosofico.it, 'Il Candelaio, la summa dell'arte e della filosofia di Giordano Bruno'

stops.name: Paris, De compendiosa architectura and the departure for England
stops.campa: Before he leaves, Bruno prints one further book at Gourbin's press, De compendiosa architectura et complemento artis Lulli, his most direct homage to the Catalan master whose wheels he has carried since Teofilo da Vairano's rooms in Naples. Then, commended by Henri III himself with letters to his ambassador in London, Michel de Castelnau, Sieur de Mauvissière, Bruno crosses the Channel, not as a fugitive this time but as a scholar traveling under royal protection, to a Protestant island where a new and freer air is said to blow.
suggested_refs: De compendiosa architectura et complemento artis Lulli, Paris 1582, Bruno's fullest tribute to Ramon Llull
sources: Marco Matteoli, 'Ars combinatoria and Ars memoriae in Giordano Bruno'

segments.name: London and the Ash Wednesday Supper

stops.name: London, the house of the French ambassador
stops.campa: Bruno lodges in the London house of Michel de Castelnau at Salisbury Court, guest and unofficial secretary of the French embassy, and moves for the first time in years in a circle that does not merely tolerate but courts him: the poet-courtier Philip Sidney, the translator John Florio, gentlemen curious about the new Copernican astronomy and the older Hermetic wisdom alike. Elizabeth's London, Protestant and half-Italianate, gives him the freedom to write in his own Italian rather than the schoolmen's Latin, and in this house he composes, within two years, the six dialogues that are his masterwork.
suggested_refs: The French embassy at Salisbury Court, London, Bruno's home for two years
sources: Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition

stops.name: Oxford, the disputation before the Polish prince
stops.campa: Invited to Oxford in the train of the visiting Polish Prince Albert Łaski, Bruno disputes publicly with the university doctors, defending the Copernican motion of the earth and an infinity of worlds against the fixed Aristotelian heaven the dons have taught for three centuries. His opponent, Doctor Underhill, and the assembled masters answer less with argument than with laughter at his accent and his gestures, and then with the graver charge of plagiarism, tracing his most exact citations to Ficino's own words on love and light. He leaves Oxford scorned, and famous.
stops.quote: Pedantic, obstinate ignorance and presumption, mixed with rustic incivility.
stops.quote_source: La cena de le ceneri (1584), Bruno on the Oxford doctors
suggested_refs: The University Church of St Mary the Virgin, Oxford, site of the 1583 disputation
sources: Frances Yates, 'Giordano Bruno's Conflict with Oxford'
Shakespeare Oxford Fellowship, 'Giordano Bruno: Mad, Bad and Dangerous to Know'

stops.name: Whitehall, the Supper on Ash Wednesday
stops.campa: On the eve of Lent, Sir Fulke Greville, in chambers near Whitehall, gathers Bruno with two Oxford doctors, Torquato and Nundinio, the translator Florio, and a company of gentlemen for a supper that becomes the frame of Bruno's own account: through darkened streets without torches, across a filthy Thames-side path, to a table where the Copernican universe is argued over wine while the Oxford men, in Bruno's telling, answer with pedantry and bad Latin rather than reasoned philosophy. He will make of this single evening the setting for his first and greatest Italian dialogue.
stops.quote: Time is the father of truth, its mother is our mind.
suggested_refs: Fulke Greville's chambers near Whitehall, setting of the Ash Wednesday Supper of La Cena de le Ceneri

stops.name: London, La Cena de le Ceneri and De la causa printed
stops.campa: Bruno publishes La Cena de le Ceneri, the Ash Wednesday Supper, dedicated to Castelnau, the first of the Italian dialogues, in which the earth turns, the sun is a star among others, and the Oxford doctors' Latin pedantry stands condemned beside the new cosmology. Within months follows De la causa, principio et uno, On Cause, Principle and Unity, in which the created world and its infinite divine cause are declared, against the schools, one same substance seen from within and from without: the universe is an animal, and God its indwelling soul, not a carpenter standing outside his work.
stops.quote: The universe is one, infinite, immobile.
stops.quote_source: De la causa, principio et uno, dialogue V (1584)
suggested_refs: La Cena de le Ceneri and De la causa, principio et uno, London 1584

stops.name: London, De l'infinito universo e mondi and the Beast Expelled
stops.campa: The cosmology reaches its full statement in De l'infinito, universo e mondi, On the Infinite Universe and Worlds: no wall of crystal spheres bounds creation, but numberless suns burn in numberless systems across a space without edge or center, each perhaps peopled with its own worlds. In the same year comes Lo spaccio de la bestia trionfante, The Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast, an allegorical reform of the heavens in which the old vice-gods are voted out of the sky by a council of virtues, dedicated, like the Furori that will follow, to Sir Philip Sidney.
stops.quote: There are then innumerable suns, and an infinite number of earths revolve around these suns.
stops.quote_source: De l'infinito, universo e mondi, first dialogue (1584)
suggested_refs: De l'infinito, universo e mondi, London 1584, the innumerable suns and innumerable earths
sources: Britannica, 'On the Infinite Universe and Worlds'

stops.name: London, De gli eroici furori and the parting from Sidney's England
stops.campa: The last of the London dialogues, De gli eroici furori, The Heroic Frenzies, closes the cycle: a sequence of love-sonnets read as an allegory of the soul's furious ascent toward the infinite One, dedicated once more to Philip Sidney. Within the year Castelnau is recalled to France and Bruno's protection with him; he sails back across the Channel he crossed two years before as an unknown foreigner and now leaves as the author of six Italian books that will outlast every court that heard him, though almost none of them yet grasp what he has actually said about the shape of the world.
suggested_refs: De gli eroici furori, London 1585, printed by John Charlewood, dedicated to Philip Sidney

segments.name: The German Courts: Paris Again, Marburg, Wittenberg, Prague

stops.name: Paris, the disputation of the Collège de Cambrai and the riot
stops.campa: Back in Paris with Castelnau, Bruno stages one last public battle with the schools: at the Collège de Cambrai, before the royal lecturers, his disciple Jean Hennequin reads out a hundred and twenty articles against Aristotelian physics under Bruno's own direction. The hall dissolves into uproar; the League's Catholic party, already suspicious of any Italian too close to a Protestant queen's ambassador, and the Peripatetic faculty alike turn on him, and within weeks, with Paris sliding toward the violence of the Guises, Bruno judges France no longer safe and rides east for the Rhine and the Protestant universities of the Empire.
suggested_refs: The Camoeracensis Acrotismus, Wittenberg 1588, Bruno's revised account of the Cambrai disputation
sources: vitadibruno.filosofia.sns.it, 'La disputa al Collège de Cambrai'

stops.name: Marburg, one day's registration and a night's refusal
stops.campa: At Marburg on the Lahn, the university register notes, in a clerk's careful Latin, the enrollment of Giordano of Nola, doctor of Rome in sacred theology, on the twenty-fifth of July. But the welcome sours quickly; whatever the exact quarrel, within days he is refused the ordinary courtesies of the philosophy faculty and moves on without ceremony, one more brief and bitter stop on a road now measured less in miles than in universities that will not quite have him.
stops.quote: Giordano of Naples of Nola, doctor of theology of Rome.
stops.quote_source: Matriculation register of the University of Marburg, 25 July 1586
suggested_refs: The matriculation register of the University of Marburg, entry of 25 July 1586
sources: archive.org, 'Vita di Giordano Bruno: con documenti editi e inediti'

stops.name: Wittenberg, welcomed at Luther's own university
stops.campa: Wittenberg, the Leucorea, cradle of the Reformation, receives him where Marburg would not: for nearly two years he lectures freely on logic, the Organon, and his own Lullian art, publishing De lampade combinatoria Lulliana and the Camoeracensis Acrotismus, revisiting the Paris disputation with the schools now safely behind him. He calls these the happiest months of his exile, a rare peace among Lutheran scholars willing, for once, to let a heterodox Italian teach without denouncing him within the week.
suggested_refs: De lampade combinatoria Lulliana, Wittenberg 1587, Bruno's Lullian logic

stops.name: Wittenberg, the farewell oration in praise of Luther
stops.campa: When a change of rector brings a stricter Calvinist orthodoxy to the Leucorea and Bruno's welcome cools, he delivers, on the eighth of March, his Oratio valedictoria before the assembled faculty and students: an eloquent, almost startling tribute to Martin Luther's courage in breaking Rome's yoke, woven, in the classicist's habit, with an unacknowledged debt to Rabelais, and closing in heartfelt gratitude to the German nation that gave a hunted Italian two years of undisturbed work. He leaves Wittenberg still speaking well of it, one of the few places in this exile he will not curse.
suggested_refs: The Oratio valedictoria, Bruno's farewell address at Wittenberg, 8 March 1588
sources: Gerardo Picardo, Giordano Bruno: Due Orazioni

stops.name: Prague, the dedication to Rudolf II and the hoped-for chair
stops.campa: Bruno comes to Prague and the strange, alchemical court of Emperor Rudolf II, collector of Hermetists, clockmakers, and cabalists, and dedicates to him the Articuli centum et sexaginta adversus huius tempestatis mathematicos atque philosophos, a hundred and sixty articles attacking the geometers of the age, prefaced by a letter urging religious tolerance as the only medicine for Europe's wars. Rudolf, delighted but noncommittal, rewards him with three hundred thalers and no chair; after six months of hoping for an imperial post that never comes, Bruno moves on again, deeper into the Empire.
suggested_refs: The Articuli centum et sexaginta, Prague 1588, dedicated to Rudolf II
sources: cafeboheme.cz, 'Giordano Bruno, an heretic in the royal court of Rudolf II'

segments.name: Helmstedt, Frankfurt, and Zurich: the Last Books

stops.name: Helmstedt, the Academy Julia and the great Latin poems
stops.campa: In January he matriculates at the small Julius-University of Helmstedt, and under the protection of the Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel Bruno finds a last quiet corner of Germany and begins the three vast Latin poems that will be his final and most systematic testament: De triplici minimo et mensura, De monade numero et figura, De immenso et innumerabilibus, on the minimum unit of being, the monad as the number underlying all number, and the boundless universe restated now in hexameters rather than Italian prose, an old philosopher-poet's summa of everything he has taught since Naples.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt trilogy in manuscript: De triplici minimo, De monade, De immenso, begun at Helmstedt

stops.name: Helmstedt, excommunicated a second time
stops.campa: Within weeks of his matriculation, Gilbert Voët, superintendent of the Lutheran church at Helmstedt, excommunicates Bruno from the communion, for reasons Bruno himself will call private and never fully explain; who exactly pronounced the ban is still argued over by scholars. It is the second time in a decade a Christian church has cast him out, after Geneva's Calvinists ten years before, and it will not be the last: he is fast becoming, without quite intending the distinction, the one philosopher of his century expelled in turn from Rome, from Calvin's Geneva, and now from Luther's own faculty, for the crime of agreeing entirely with none of them.
suggested_refs: Helmstedt 1589: wer exkommunizierte Giordano Bruno? — the scholarship on Bruno's Lutheran excommunication
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico, 'Bruno, Giordano' (names Gilbert Voët)
Pietro Daniel Omodeo, 'Helmstedt 1589: wer exkommunizierte Giordano Bruno?', Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte (2011)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the book fair and the trilogy in print
stops.campa: Bruno settles for a season at Frankfurt am Main, lodging with the Carmelite friars, and works with the printers Johann Wechel and Peter Fischer to bring out the trilogy begun at Helmstedt: De triplici minimo, De monade, De immenso, printed in 1591 in time for the great autumn Book Fair that draws buyers and sellers from every printing house in Europe. The city magistrates, wary of the itinerant Italian's reputation, will shortly order him to leave, but not before the fair has scattered his boldest cosmology across the trade routes of Christendom in Latin hexameters few outside the learned will ever fully parse.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt Book Fair of 1591, where De triplici minimo, De monade, and De immenso were sold

stops.name: Zurich, lectures for Hainzel and Egli
stops.campa: Ordered from Frankfurt, Bruno winters instead in Zurich, invited by the patrician Johann Heinrich Hainzel and the theologian Raphael Egli to give a private course of lectures on scholastic metaphysics; Egli will later gather and publish the notes as Summa terminorum metaphysicorum. It is a modest, almost domestic interlude, teaching for a small circle of Swiss admirers, the last calm room before the invitation that will undo him arrives by letter from a city he has not yet troubled to visit: Venice.
suggested_refs: Summa terminorum metaphysicorum, Zurich lectures published by Raphael Egli, 1595

stops.name: Frankfurt, the bookseller Ciotto and Mocenigo's letter
stops.campa: Back in Frankfurt in the spring, Bruno is found by the Venetian bookseller Giovanni Battista Ciotto, an old acquaintance from the fair, who carries a letter from a young Venetian patrician, Giovanni Mocenigo: enthralled by report of Bruno's art of memory, Mocenigo begs him to come and reside at his own expense in Venice and there be instructed. It is an offer of a patron, a roof, a fixed address after eight years of German lodging houses; against every instinct that has kept him one step ahead of the Roman Inquisition since 1576, Bruno accepts, and turns south, back into Italy, for the first time in fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The letter of Giovanni Mocenigo, carried by Giovanni Battista Ciotto, that drew Bruno back to Italy

stops.name: Venice, the Palazzo Mocenigo at San Samuele
stops.campa: Bruno arrives in Venice and takes lodging as promised in Mocenigo's own palace at San Samuele on the Grand Canal, engaged to teach his patron the art of memory and, it becomes clear within weeks, a good deal more: the infinite universe, the plurality of worlds, a philosophy of nature that treats miracle and dogma alike as figures for deeper truths. Mocenigo listens hungrily at first, boasting of his new tutor to friends, unaware or unwilling yet to reckon what such teaching will cost a man of his own rank should it ever reach the Holy Office.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Mocenigo at San Samuele, Venice, where Bruno lodged as Giovanni Mocenigo's guest
sources: serenissima.news, 'Rosolina: i Mocenigo e l'eretico Giordano Bruno'

stops.name: Padua, the vacant chair that went instead to Galileo
stops.campa: Hearing the chair of mathematics at the University of Padua stands empty, Bruno goes there in late summer, gives a private course of lectures to German students, and composes the Praelectiones geometricae and the Ars deformationum in hope of the appointment. By the onset of winter it is plain the chair will not be his; in 1592 it is given instead to a thirty-year-old professor from Pisa named Galileo Galilei, who will hold it for eighteen years. Bruno returns to Venice and to Mocenigo's house disappointed, the two careers crossing once in Padua and never again.
suggested_refs: The chair of mathematics at the University of Padua, vacant in 1591, given to Galileo in 1592

stops.name: Venice, Mocenigo's disappointment and the locked attic
stops.campa: Back at San Samuele through the spring, Mocenigo grows convinced he is not being taught the secret arts he paid for and that his guest holds back the deepest doctrines; pressed by his own confessor and by disappointment curdling into suspicion, he acts. On the night of the twenty-second of May he has servants lock Bruno into an attic room of the palace, and the next day carries the first of what will become three depositions to the Inquisitor of Venice, laying out, sentence by remembered sentence, the philosopher's private table-talk on an eternal universe, a movable earth, and a Christ who worked no true miracles.
suggested_refs: Mocenigo's first denunciation to the Venetian Inquisition, 23 May 1592
sources: alessandrodiadamo.wordpress.com, 'Il processo a Giordano Bruno. La denuncia di Giovanni Mocenigo'

stops.name: Venice, arrest and the cells of San Domenico di Castello
stops.campa: In the night of the twenty-third to twenty-fourth of May, Captain Matteo d'Avanzo takes Bruno into custody on the Inquisitor's warrant and lodges him in the cells of the Holy Office at San Domenico di Castello. Mocenigo, not yet satisfied, brings a second denunciation on the twenty-fifth, handing over Bruno's own books seized from the palace, and a third on the twenty-ninth, now accusing him outright of reviling the Roman Church and its sacraments. The Venetian Inquisition, more temperate than Rome's, begins a methodical, almost gentle questioning that will run through the summer and autumn.
suggested_refs: The cells of the Holy Office at San Domenico di Castello, Venice, Bruno's first prison
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

stops.name: Venice, the trial and Rome's demand for extradition
stops.campa: Through months of Venetian interrogation Bruno answers with unusual candor, admitting doubts on transubstantiation and the Trinity while insisting he is a philosopher testing truth by natural reason, not a heretic denying the faith outright; he even offers partial retraction, hoping Venice's milder tribunal will settle the matter locally. But Rome, informed of so celebrated a fugitive, formally demands his extradition, citing the still-open Neapolitan file of 1576. The Venetian Senate, however jealous of its own jurisdiction, yields in January to the Holy See's insistence, and Bruno is delivered by galley to the Roman Inquisition to answer, at last, for everything since his flight from San Domenico Maggiore.
suggested_refs: The extradition order of February 1593, transferring Bruno from Venice to the Roman Inquisition
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

segments.name: Rome: the Cells and the Fire

stops.name: Rome, delivered to the Sant'Uffizio
stops.campa: Bruno is landed at Rome and lodged in the prison of the Holy Office by the Vatican, beginning what will become nearly eight unbroken years of confinement, the longest of any prisoner of the Roman Inquisition in that generation. The dossier assembled against him is now vast: the Naples file of 1576, the Venetian depositions of Mocenigo and of Bruno's own hand, and the printed evidence of a dozen books arguing an eternal, infinite, ensouled universe, a plurality of inhabited worlds, and a Christ read as a great magus rather than the unique incarnate God of the Creed.
suggested_refs: The prison of the Sant'Uffizio at the Vatican, Bruno's cell for nearly eight years
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

stops.name: Rome, the commission of theologians examines the books
stops.campa: A commission of theologians, appointed to comb every surviving work for censurable propositions, spends years reducing the sprawl of Bruno's Italian dialogues and Latin poems to a list of specific heresies: the eternity of the world, the infinity of inhabited worlds, the transmigration of souls, the denial of a real distinction between the divine persons, magic and Hermetic practice mixed with natural philosophy. Bruno, examined repeatedly across these years, answers with a philosopher's patience at first, distinguishing at every turn between what he holds as demonstrated by reason and what remains, he insists, a matter of faith he does not presume to touch.
suggested_refs: The censure commission's list of propositions drawn from Bruno's collected works, 1596-1599
sources: Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

stops.name: Rome, Bellarmine's eight propositions and the refusal
stops.campa: In January the congregation approves the eight capital propositions to which the Jesuit Cardinal Roberto Bellarmine has reduced the whole case, and urges Bruno to abjure them, the last and gentlest offer of a way out the Church will make him. Bruno at first asks time to consider, and for months the case hangs in truce. But on the twenty-first of December he tells his examiners flatly that he has nothing to retract, does not know what he should retract, and does not recognize himself as a heretic at all: he is a philosopher pursuing truth, not a theologian bound by dogma he has never claimed to teach as revelation.
stops.quote: I neither ought to retract, nor will I retract; nor have I matter for which to retract.
stops.quote_source: Roman trial record, deposition of 21 December 1599
suggested_refs: Cardinal Bellarmine's eight censured propositions, presented to Bruno in 1599
sources: ultimavoce.it, 'Giordano Bruno, l'ostinato eretico bruciato vivo dalla Chiesa'
Luigi Firpo, Il processo di Giordano Bruno

stops.name: Rome, Clement VIII orders the sentence
stops.campa: With the accused's final and formal refusal on record, the matter passes to Pope Clement VIII himself, who on the twentieth of January orders that Bruno be handed over to the secular arm as an impenitent and pertinacious heretic, the formula that seals a sentence of death by fire, since the Church may condemn a soul but will not itself shed blood. Eight years of imprisonment, examination, and negotiated silence end in this single administrative line; the philosopher who has evaded every court of Europe since 1576 has, in the end, refused the one door still open to him.
suggested_refs: Pope Clement VIII's order of 20 January 1600, remanding Bruno to the secular arm
sources: ultimavoce.it, 'Giordano Bruno, l'ostinato eretico bruciato vivo dalla Chiesa'

stops.name: Rome, the sentence read and 'greater fear'
stops.campa: Taken from the cells of the Sant'Uffizio and led to the palace of Cardinal Ludovico Madruzzo beside Piazza Navona, Bruno kneels before the assembled cardinal inquisitors, stripped of every clerical dignity, while the sentence of the Holy Office is read at length: heretic, relapsed, impenitent, obstinate, to be degraded and delivered to the governor of Rome for punishment as mild as possible and without shedding of blood, the Inquisition's grim euphemism for burning. Rising from his knees, Bruno turns on his judges the sentence that will outlive every one of their names.
stops.quote: Maiori forsan cum timore sententiam in me fertis quam ego accipiam.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Gaspar Schoppe, letter to Konrad Rittershausen, 17 February 1600
suggested_refs: The palace of Cardinal Ludovico Madruzzo near Piazza Navona, Rome, where the sentence of 8 February 1600 was pronounced
sources: grandeoriente.it, '8 febbraio 1600: Giordano Bruno viene condannato al rogo'
Gaspar Schoppe, letter to Rittershausen, 17 February 1600

stops.name: Rome, Campo de' Fiori, the fire
stops.campa: At dawn on the seventeenth of February, in the year of the Church's great jubilee, Bruno is led through Rome to Campo de' Fiori with his tongue bound in a gag of wood and iron, that he preach no last heresy to the crowd, stripped, and bound to a stake atop the pyre. A crucifix is held up before his face as the flame is set; Schoppe, watching, records that Bruno thrusts the image away with a fierce look. He dies at fifty-two, having refused every court, every creed, and every offered mercy that asked him to unsay what he had seen.
stops.quote: When the image of our crucified Saviour was shown to him before his death, he thrust it away with a fierce look.
stops.quote_source: Gaspar Schoppe, letter to Konrad Rittershausen, 17 February 1600
suggested_refs: Ettore Ferrari's 1889 bronze of Giordano Bruno, standing today on Campo de' Fiori facing the Vatican
sources: Gaspar Schoppe, letter to Rittershausen, 17 February 1600
